newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Catastrophes cost insurers 22 percent less in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Catastrophes cost insurers 22 percent less in 1996.

text.p: Worldwide insurance losses from natural and man-made disasters fell 22 percent to $12.3 billion last year, with the United States accounting for 64 percent, Swiss Reinsurance Co. said Tuesday.

Natural disasters accounted for the larger share of the total damage with $7.9 billion, including the year's largest single loss of $1.6 billion from hurricane Fran in the U.S. Southeast in September.
Storms and freezing weather in the United States produced 11 of last year's 20 most costly insurance losses from disasters, Swiss Re said in the latest issue of its Sigma research report.
"The U.S., therefore, accounted for 64 percent of global insured losses," Sigma said.
Catastrophes caused $12.3 billion in insured losses in 1996, out of a total of $50 billion, including damage not backed by insurers, according to Sigma.
"The past year may, therefore, be regarded as a continuation of the record series experienced since 1989, with total claims in excess of $12 billion," Sigma said.
"Within this record series, however, 1996 did show the lowest claim level, as losses from natural catastrophes were relatively low," it added.
The most devestating natural catastrophes happened in Asia, including two periods of Chinese flooding that killed 2,700 people, but produced few claims due to a low level of insurance.

Man-made disasters accounted for $4.4 billion in losses, led by five cases totalling $2 billion -- fires at Credit Lyonnais headquarters, in the tunnel under the English Channel and at Duesseldorf Airport in Germany as well as two bomb attacks in London and Manchester, England.
Sigma's report on 1996 covered 341 catastrophes that claimed a total of 22,000 lives.
It said Asia was a high risk region with 50 percent of all 1996 catastrophes and 70 percent of resulting fatalities. But low insurance levels meant Asia only acounted for one-tenth of world losses.
"The reverse situation applies to the U.S./Europe, with its high degree of insurance: insured losses are high, despite a lower exposure to catastrophes," Sigma wrote.

The number of disasters overall had risen continuouslsy since 1970 due in part to more detailed information but also to higher population density, broader coverage for assets and a concentration of assets in industrial nations, Sigma wrote.
